title: Make Hub feel at home in your organisation
description: A practical overview of custom styling, brand assets, translations and email templates.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional service provider wanting Hub to match the rest of its customer portal. Does that mean rebuilding the frontend for every colour change?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The documented approach injects custom styling and assets into the frontend container through mounted storage. Keep those custom files separate and wire the mounts through the Helm deployment, using the expected paths.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So the important work is both the asset and the deployment wiring?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. A beautiful stylesheet sitting in the wrong directory has no effect. Use browser inspection to choose targeted overrides and check the result after deployment, including contrast and readable controls.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can our provider put its logo, icons and browser tab image into one random folder?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not quite. The logo uses the documented sidebar SVG name, icons follow the expected SVG library structure, and favicons have a separate location and mount. Each is a small contract that the application already understands.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What would you verify beyond the login page?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Check the signed-in sidebar, the icons used in real workflows and the browser tab. Branding is more convincing when it remains legible across the interface instead of looking correct in just one screenshot.

chapters.title: Change wording without copying every translation

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The provider calls its dashboard a command centre. Must it maintain a complete new language file?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Custom translation files can override only the keys you want to change. Missing keys retain the shipped translations. Match the expected language filenames and nested key structure, and use the built-in English file as a reference.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That sounds easier to maintain during upgrades.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It is a narrower responsibility. Check the actual pages using your changed labels, and test each customised language. Don't replace a whole shipped translation set when a small override is enough.

chapters.title: Email has its own branding surface

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Is the job done when the web application looks right?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Remember the emails. Custom templates have their own mount, filenames, subjects and available variables. Templates you don't supply keep their built-in defaults. A mismatched configured template name can also leave you seeing the default instead of your custom version.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should our provider send as a final check?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Representative messages for each customised email type. Use only variables available to that email, because a missing value can remain as literal placeholder text. Verify the subject, links and both content variants, not just the logo.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
